transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Hi. Yeah, it’s... it’s good to meet you too. I guess what brings me in is, well, I just can’t keep my words in a straight line anymore. Like, at all. I work as an orderly—a psych aide, actually, mostly doing the overnight shifts because I thought the nights would be a little slower, you know, just doing rounds and helping out when things get loud. But lately, I’ll be trying to talk to the charge nurse, just starting to tell her about how the overnight shift went, and before I even realize what’s happening, my brain just... it completely derails. 

I'll start on the shift report and then I end up jumping to talking about soccer, like this match I saw before I clocked in, and then somehow I'm going on and on about the paint colors on the walls in the dayroom—because they painted it this awful sterile yellow last month and it's been bugging me—and then I'm suddenly talking about the patient charts again, but it’s all mixed up and out of order. And I can just look at the nurses, or my friends, or whoever I'm talking to, and I can see everyone getting completely lost. Their eyes just sort of glaze over or they look at me like I'm speaking a different language. And the worst part is I know I'm doing it, I know I'm not making sense, but the words just keep spilling out in this huge tangled mess and I can't put them back in order no matter how hard I try to just focus and say the one simple thing I meant to say in the first place. It's just exhausting.
Have there been times when you felt unusually high, energized, or unstoppable?

Unstoppable? No, man, definitely not. I mean, I wish, right? But no. If anything, it’s the exact opposite. I never get that feeling where I’m buzzing or feeling like I can take on the world or do a million things at once. I see it sometimes, you know, on the ward—patients who are just bouncing off the walls, or even some of the other aides who pound like three energy drinks before midnight and they’re just zooming through the halls, talking about how they're going to start a business or whatever. But me? I never feel high or energized like that. 

Honestly, most of the time I feel like I’m walking through wet cement. Just getting out of bed when my alarm goes off at 9 PM for the night shift... I just lie there staring at the ceiling, and my arms and legs feel like they weigh a hundred pounds each. It takes everything I have just to put my scrubs on and tie my shoes. I can barely find the energy to pack a sandwich for my break, let alone feel unstoppable. It’s just this constant, heavy slog, like my battery is always at one percent, no matter how much I sleep or what I do. Even when I was younger, in high school, I wasn't exactly the hyper type, but now it's just... heavy. All the time. So, yeah, no, I’ve never had times like what you're saying. Not even close.
Have you been hearing voices or sounds that other people don’t seem to hear?

Voices? No, no, I don't... I don't hear anything like that. I mean, don't get me wrong, where I work, it’s never actually quiet, even at three in the morning. You’d think the night shift would be silent, right? But it’s just this constant, low hum all night long. You’ve got the HVAC system rattling in the ceiling above the nurses' station, and the ice machine down the hall in the breakroom that kicks on randomly and sounds exactly like someone dropping a bag of rocks. And, you know, sometimes you hear the patients muttering in their sleep or pacing around in their socks on the linoleum. 

So there are always sounds around me. Sometimes I'll be sitting there, just staring at the computer screen trying to keep my eyes open, and I'll hear a thump, and I have to go walk all the way down the east wing to check if someone fell out of bed or dropped a book. But it's always something real, you know? It's always just the building settling, or a door clicking shut because the draft caught it, or one of the other aides dropping a clipboard. It’s never, like, voices in my head or someone whispering my name when no one is there. 

I know some of the patients I watch over, they deal with that a lot, and they'll tell me about the people talking to them from the air vents or the smoke detectors. I always sit and listen to them, and I feel really bad because I can see how terrified they get, but I just don't experience that myself. Even when I clock out and go home to my apartment, it's just the normal stuff—the traffic out on the street, the guy in the apartment upstairs walking around in heavy boots at noon when I'm trying to sleep. My brain might be a complete tangled mess when I try to string a sentence together, like I was saying before, and I feel like I'm dragging a ton of bricks around every single day, but it’s not making up sounds. It's just... quiet in my head in that specific way. Well, not quiet because of the city noise and the building noise, but you know what I mean. I definitely don't hear things that aren't actually there.
Do you believe that anyone is trying to harm you or control you?

Well... I mean, harm me? I don't know if they want to physically hurt me, but... but they're definitely doing things to mess with me. Specifically the supervisors. The nursing directors, the shift managers, all of them up on the third floor where the administrative offices are. I know they are. I mean, they keep changing my shifts around, right? And I know, I know everyone says it’s just because we’re short-staffed. The charge nurse—Brenda, she’s been there like fifteen years—she keeps telling me, "Oh, we just need coverage because two people quit last week and someone else is on maternity leave." She says it’s just the schedule being the schedule. 

But I know that’s not the real reason. I’m absolutely sure of it. They’re moving me around on purpose. They want to keep me off balance, and... and they’re watching me. Like, constantly. We have these dome cameras all over the unit—in the hallways, pointing at the med room door, in the dayroom—and I swear, every time I walk past one, I can feel them sitting up there in their offices zooming in on me. They want to see if I’m unsafe. They’re waiting for me to make a mistake, or maybe they think I'm dangerous or something because my thoughts get so jumbled up like I was telling you before. 

I’ll be doing my fifteen-minute checks at 2 AM, just walking down the hall with my flashlight, and I look up at the camera near room 412, and I just know someone is on the other side of that lens, tracking my every move, taking notes on me. I tried to tell one of the other aides about it, this guy Marcus I usually work with, and he just laughed and said the cameras don't even record half the time and nobody watches them live unless there's a code. But he doesn't get it. He doesn't see how the schedule changes always line up with when they want to observe me. They're trying to prove something about me. They want to control where I am and when I'm there so they can monitor me perfectly. I just... I know they are. It's not just staffing shortages. It's me. They're watching me.
Have you had any recent head injury, seizure, or other medical illness around the time these problems started?

No, no, nothing like that. I haven't hit my head or anything. I mean, the last time I really hurt myself was probably back in middle school when I fell off my bike and scraped my knee up pretty bad, but definitely no head injuries. And seizures? No, I've never had a seizure. I know what those look like, too, because we get patients on the unit sometimes who have seizure disorders, and you have to be really careful with them, making sure they don't hit their heads on the floor or the furniture if they go down. We have a whole protocol for it, rolling them on their side, timing it, all that. But me? No, never. 

And as for other medical illnesses... I mean, I'm generally pretty healthy, physically speaking. I don't have diabetes or high blood pressure or anything like that. I had a cold a couple of months ago, you know, just a regular runny nose and a cough that lingered for a week or two, probably caught it from someone on the ward because germs spread like wildfire in there with everyone in such close quarters. But that was just a standard cold, nothing serious. I took some over-the-counter stuff and drank a lot of orange juice, and it cleared right up. 

But around the time all this started? The heaviness, the thoughts getting all tangled, the supervisors watching me on the cameras? No, there wasn't any sickness or injury. It wasn't like I got the flu and then suddenly my brain felt like it was walking through wet cement. It just sort of... happened. Like a slow leak in a tire, you know? You don't notice it at first, and then one day you're just driving on the rim. But no doctor has ever told me I have a brain tumor or a thyroid problem or anything that would cause all this. I had a physical for work when I got hired, and they checked my blood and everything, and they said I was perfectly fine to start. So physically, medically, I'm fine. It's just... everything else that's a mess.
How long have these problems been going on?

How long? Um... well, if I really sit down and try to trace it back, try to figure out exactly when I started feeling like I was dragging all those bricks around, and when my thoughts started getting all jumbled up... it’s been about a year and five months. Yeah, roughly a year and five months. 

Because I remember exactly what was happening right around that time. See, when I first started at the hospital, everything was fine. I was on steady day shifts. It was a really good routine, you know? I’d go in at 7 AM, help get the patients up for breakfast, do the morning vitals, and I’d be clocking out by 3:30. I had a normal life, a normal sleep schedule. But then, they completely flipped everything on me. They switched my job from those steady days to rotating nights, and they started piling on all this overtime. 

And I mean a lot of overtime. One week I’d be doing three 12-hour night shifts, the next week they’d have me bouncing between evening shifts and overnight shifts, pulling 50 or 60 hours. You never even know what day of the week it is when you work like that, you know? You wake up at 4 in the afternoon, the sun is already starting to go down, and you just feel... drained before you even put your scrubs on. And that’s exactly when all these problems started. Right after they forced me onto those rotating nights and all that overtime. That’s when the heaviness set in, and that's when I started really noticing the schedule changes and the supervisors using the cameras to watch me, because suddenly I was there at all these weird hours when the hospital is mostly empty. I just haven't been able to shake it since they made that switch. It's been a straight year and five months of just... feeling like this.
For at least one month, have you been convinced that your supervisors were watching you through the cameras?

At least a month? Oh, wow, yeah, way more than a month. If we're just talking about the cameras, like, me knowing for a fact that they're watching me through them? And... and also my actions getting all, I guess, disorganized because my thoughts are so jumbled up? That specific part has been happening for about a year and one month. 

Because, like I was saying before, the schedule change and that awful, heavy, drained feeling, that all started a year and five months ago. But it took me a little while of working those crazy rotating overnight shifts to actually catch on to what the supervisors were really doing. It was maybe four months into it—so yeah, exactly a year and one month ago—that I really started noticing the lenses on the dome cameras following me down the hall. 

And it just completely messes with you, you know? Knowing you're being watched like a lab rat for a year and a month straight. It makes it so hard to just do my job normally. Like, I'll be trying to sort the patient dinner trays or do my rounds, and I get so overwhelmed by the fact that they're up there analyzing my every step that I start doing things out of order. I'll forget what room I'm supposed to be checking, or I'll put the soiled linens in the wrong bin, and my whole routine just gets completely disorganized. I'll just be standing there in the middle of the corridor holding a stack of towels, totally frozen, trying to act normal while they stare at me from the third floor. So, yeah, to answer your question, it's been a lot longer than a single month. It's been thirteen months of them just constantly monitoring me and waiting for me to crack.
Have you lost interest in spending time with other people or doing things you used to enjoy?

Loss of interest? Yeah... yeah, I guess you could say that. Actually, it's more like everything just turned gray, you know? Like all the color got sucked out of the things I used to do. 

I used to be really active, always doing something. Like, I used to sketch these big, elaborate murals. I had this whole sketchbook dedicated to just street art designs, really intricate stuff with lots of shading and perspective. I’d spend hours just sitting by the window in my apartment, listening to music, getting the lines just right. I was even talking to a buddy of mine about maybe pitching a design to a local business to paint their back wall. And I used to cook, too. Not just microwave stuff, but real cooking. I'd have my friends over on a Friday night, and I'd make these massive batches of enchiladas or homemade pizza from scratch. We’d hang out, eat, watch movies. It was... it was a good time. And on weekends, almost every Saturday, I’d be out at the park playing pickup soccer. I was pretty good at midfield, always running, always in the thick of it. 

But now? Now... I can't even remember the last time I opened my sketchbook. The pencils are just sitting there on my desk, gathering dust, and looking at them just makes me feel exhausted. And cooking? Forget it. The thought of chopping vegetables or standing over a stove just feels so incredibly pointless. Like, what's the point of going through all that effort just to eat something that tastes like ash in my mouth anyway? 

And my friends... they still text me sometimes. They’ll ask if I want to come kick the ball around, or if I want to grab a drink, or just come over and hang out. But I just look at the messages on my phone, and I can't even bring myself to type a reply. I just ignore them. I leave them on read, or I don't even open them at all. I just stay in my apartment. I lock the door, close the blinds so no one can look in, and I just sit there. The idea of going out, of trying to pretend I'm okay, of trying to run up and down a field or make conversation over dinner... it’s just too much. It’s like climbing a mountain with a boulder strapped to my back. So I just don't do it anymore. I just stay inside where it's quiet, even though the quiet doesn't really help. It's just easier than trying to care about things I don't care about anymore.

I had a normal life, a normal sleep schedule. But then, they completely flipped everything on me. They switched my job from those steady days to rotating nights, and they started piling on all this overtime. 

And I mean a lot of overtime. One week I’d be doing three 12-hour night shifts, the next week they’d have me bouncing between evening shifts and overnight shifts, pulling 50 or 60 hours. You never even know what day of the week it is when you work like that, you know? You wake up at 4 in the afternoon, the sun is already starting to go down, and you just feel... drained before you even put your scrubs on. And that’s exactly when all these problems started. Right after they forced me onto those rotating nights and all that overtime. That’s when the heaviness set in, and that's when I started really noticing the schedule changes and the supervisors using the cameras to watch me, because suddenly I was there at all these weird hours when the hospital is mostly empty. I just haven't been able to shake it since they made that switch. It's been a straight year and five months of just... feeling like this.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the psychotic symptoms have persisted for at least one month independent of the shift-change stressor, which helps distinguish schizophrenia from unspecified/nonorganic psychosis and psychosis due to another medical condition.
doctor.question: For at least one month, have you been convinced that your supervisors were watching you through the cameras?

target_item.name: Psychotic Symptoms Duration
target_item.manifestation: The beliefs about being watched and the disorganized behavior have been happening for about 1 year and 1 month.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking how long the beliefs about being watched by supervisors through cameras have been occurring, specifically asking if it has been at least one month, which corresponds to the duration of psychotic symptoms.

patient.answer:
At least a month? Oh, wow, yeah, way more than a month. If we're just talking about the cameras, like, me knowing for a fact that they're watching me through them? And... and also my actions getting all, I guess, disorganized because my thoughts are so jumbled up? That specific part has been happening for about a year and one month. 

Because, like I was saying before, the schedule change and that awful, heavy, drained feeling, that all started a year and five months ago. But it took me a little while of working those crazy rotating overnight shifts to actually catch on to what the supervisors were really doing. It was maybe four months into it—so yeah, exactly a year and one month ago—that I really started noticing the lenses on the dome cameras following me down the hall. 

And it just completely messes with you, you know? Knowing you're being watched like a lab rat for a year and a month straight. It makes it so hard to just do my job normally. Like, I'll be trying to sort the patient dinner trays or do my rounds, and I get so overwhelmed by the fact that they're up there analyzing my every step that I start doing things out of order. I'll forget what room I'm supposed to be checking, or I'll put the soiled linens in the wrong bin, and my whole routine just gets completely disorganized. I'll just be standing there in the middle of the corridor holding a stack of towels, totally frozen, trying to act normal while they stare at me from the third floor. So, yeah, to answer your question, it's been a lot longer than a single month. It's been thirteen months of them just constantly monitoring me and waiting for me to crack.

inference.note: Ruled out F06.2 based on no head injury, seizures, or medical illness temporally associated with onset. Duration >1 month of delusional/persecutory beliefs plus disorganized speech/behavior and negative symptoms supports a primary psychotic disorder, with schizophrenia more likely than unspecified psychosis.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there have been prominent negative symptoms, which would support schizophrenia rather than unspecified psychosis.
doctor.question: Have you lost interest in spending time with other people or doing things you used to enjoy?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Interest
target_item.manifestation: I used to sketch murals, cook for my friends, and play soccer on weekends, but now all of that feels pointless and I usually just ignore messages and stay in my apartment.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking if I have lost interest in activities I used to enjoy or spending time with people, which matches the Loss of Interest symptom.

patient.answer:
Loss of interest? Yeah... yeah, I guess you could say that. Actually, it's more like everything just turned gray, you know? Like all the color got sucked out of the things I used to do. 

I used to be really active, always doing something. Like, I used to sketch these big, elaborate murals. I had this whole sketchbook dedicated to just street art designs, really intricate stuff with lots of shading and perspective. I’d spend hours just sitting by the window in my apartment, listening to music, getting the lines just right. I was even talking to a buddy of mine about maybe pitching a design to a local business to paint their back wall. And I used to cook, too. Not just microwave stuff, but real cooking. I'd have my friends over on a Friday night, and I'd make these massive batches of enchiladas or homemade pizza from scratch. We’d hang out, eat, watch movies. It was... it was a good time. And on weekends, almost every Saturday, I’d be out at the park playing pickup soccer. I was pretty good at midfield, always running, always in the thick of it. 

But now? Now... I can't even remember the last time I opened my sketchbook. The pencils are just sitting there on my desk, gathering dust, and looking at them just makes me feel exhausted. And cooking? Forget it. The thought of chopping vegetables or standing over a stove just feels so incredibly pointless. Like, what's the point of going through all that effort just to eat something that tastes like ash in my mouth anyway? 

And my friends... they still text me sometimes. They’ll ask if I want to come kick the ball around, or if I want to grab a drink, or just come over and hang out. But I just look at the messages on my phone, and I can't even bring myself to type a reply. I just ignore them. I leave them on read, or I don't even open them at all. I just stay in my apartment. I lock the door, close the blinds so no one can look in, and I just sit there. The idea of going out, of trying to pretend I'm okay, of trying to run up and down a field or make conversation over dinner... it’s just too much. It’s like climbing a mountain with a boulder strapped to my back. So I just don't do it anymore. I just stay inside where it's quiet, even though the quiet doesn't really help. It's just easier than trying to care about things I don't care about anymore.

inference.note: Duration now clearly exceeds 6 months, with at least 1 month of fixed persecutory delusions plus disorganized speech/behavior and negative symptoms; this rules out F29 as the best remaining candidate and supports schizophrenia.

opening_question.intent: Understand the patient's main concern for seeking psychiatric help today
opening_question.question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient reports over 1 year of persistent persecutory delusions (supervisors watching and controlling him through cameras and scheduling), disorganized speech/thought, and functional disorganization at work, along with prominent negative symptoms including avolition/social withdrawal/anhedonia. Symptoms have persisted well beyond 6 months, with at least 1 month of active psychotic symptoms. There is no evidence of manic episodes, no reported hallucinations, and no medical/neurological cause identified. This presentation is most consistent with schizophrenia.
